title: The nervous system and the brain

tips.title: Sensory in, relay across, motor out
tips.body: **Sensory** carries impulses **to** the CNS, **relay** passes them **across within** it, **motor** carries them **out** to an effector. Three words in that order give you the middle of every reflex arc question.

tips.title: Say diffuses, and say receptors
tips.body: At a synapse the neurotransmitter **diffuses across** the gap and **binds to receptors** on the next neurone. *Goes across* leaves out both how it travels and what happens when it arrives — and those are the two marks.

tips.title: An effector is a muscle or a gland
tips.body: Not a nerve, not a part of the brain. If a question asks you to name the effector, the answer is the **muscle** that contracts or the **gland** that secretes — and naming which muscle is better than saying *a muscle*.

tips.title: CT for structure, PET for function
tips.body: **CT** uses **X-rays** and shows **where** something is — a tumour, an area of damage. **PET** uses a **tracer** and shows **which parts are active**, so it answers *what does this region do*. Match the scan to what the question wants to know.

tips.title: The conscious brain, not the brain
tips.body: A reflex does not wait for a **conscious decision**, but the impulse **is** still sent to the brain — which is why you feel the pain afterwards. Writing *the brain is not involved* is not quite right, and the wording is marked.

why.matters:
Hormones are the slow control system; this is the fast one. An impulse travels as **electricity** along a neurone, which is why a message can cross your body in milliseconds and why it can be aimed at one muscle rather than broadcast.

The interesting design decision is that some responses **do not wait for the conscious brain**. A reflex is routed through the spinal cord, or through an unconscious part of the brain, so that nothing has to decide on it — which is the difference between a burnt finger and a burnt hand.

examples.title: Why your hand is off the pan before you notice
examples.body:
A reflex is automatic and does not involve conscious thought, and the reason is the **route**. The impulse goes from the receptor along a sensory neurone into the spinal cord, straight across a **relay neurone**, and back out along a motor neurone to the muscle.

The brain is told afterwards, which is why the pain arrives **after** the hand has moved. Going to the conscious brain and back would add distance and several synapses, and reflexes exist for exactly the situations where that delay is the damage.

visual.alt: A flow chart of the reflex arc: the hot pan is the stimulus, a receptor and sensory neurone carry it to a relay neurone in the spinal cord, and a motor neurone takes it to the muscle, which moves the hand

examples.title: Why a gap in the wiring is useful
examples.body:
Neurones do not touch. At a **synapse** the electrical impulse stops, a **neurotransmitter** is released across the gap, and a new impulse starts in the next neurone. That is slower than a wire, and it is not an accident.

A gap makes the junction one-way, so signals cannot run backwards. It lets one neurone be fed by many, so signals can be added up rather than simply passed on. And because the crossing is chemical, it is something a drug can act on — which is how many nervous-system medicines, such as antidepressants, work.

visual.alt: A flow chart of a synapse: an impulse arriving releases a neurotransmitter, which diffuses across the gap and starts a new impulse in the next neurone

examples.title: Why brain damage is so hard to treat
examples.body:
Almost every other organ can be operated on, and the brain mostly cannot. The specification asks for the **limitations**, and there are four worth having.

It is **delicate**, so any procedure risks damage. It is enclosed in the **skull**, so getting to it is a problem in itself. Drugs often cannot get in, because the **blood-brain barrier** keeps them out along with everything else. And nervous tissue does not repair like skin — damage is usually permanent, which is why prevention and rehabilitation carry so much of the weight.

steps.title: The nervous system, and what a neurone looks like
steps.body:
The nervous system carries information as **electrical impulses**, quickly and precisely.

It has two parts:

- The **central nervous system (CNS)** — the **brain** and **spinal cord**, where information is processed.
- The **peripheral nervous system** — the neurones running to and from the CNS.

Information enters the nervous system at a **sensory receptor**: a cell, or group of cells, that **detects a stimulus** and **converts it into an electrical impulse**. Light-sensitive cells in the retina and temperature receptors in the skin are examples.

**A neurone** is a nerve cell, and the specification names its parts:

- The **cell body**, containing the nucleus.
- **Dendrites**, and the longer **dendron**, which carry impulses **towards** the cell body.
- The **axon**, a long fibre carrying the impulse **away** from the cell body.
- The **myelin sheath**, a fatty layer wrapped around the axon.

The **myelin sheath** does two things, and both are worth knowing: it **insulates** the axon, stopping the impulse leaking to neighbouring neurones, and it **speeds up transmission** so the impulse travels much faster than it would along a bare fibre.

**The three kinds of neurone differ in shape as well as in job:**

- A **sensory neurone** has a **long dendron** bringing the impulse from the receptor, its **cell body part-way along**, and a **short axon** into the CNS.
- A **relay neurone** is **short**, lies wholly **inside the CNS**, and connects to many other neurones.
- A **motor neurone** has its **cell body inside the CNS**, with **many short dendrites**, and one **long axon** running out to the effector.

And neurones are **long** — a single motor neurone can run from the spinal cord to a muscle in the foot. That length is what lets an impulse cross the body without being passed between many cells.

steps.title: Synapses
steps.body:
Neurones do not touch. Where two meet there is a tiny gap called a **synapse**, and the electrical impulse cannot jump it. What happens instead is worth learning as a sequence, because it is marked as one:

1. The **electrical impulse** arrives at the end of the first neurone.
2. This causes the release of a chemical called a **neurotransmitter** into the gap.
3. The neurotransmitter **diffuses across** the synapse.
4. It **binds to receptors** on the next neurone.
5. This **triggers a new electrical impulse** in that neurone.

So the signal changes from **electrical** to **chemical** and back to **electrical**.

Two consequences follow, and questions ask for both:

- **Transmission is slowed slightly** at each synapse, because diffusion takes time. A path with many synapses is slower than one with few.
- **The signal travels one way only**, because only one side releases the neurotransmitter and only the other side has the receptors.

That one-way property is what makes a nervous system work at all: a signal that could travel either way across a junction would have no direction.

steps.title: Why reflexes are fast, and what they are for
steps.body:
**Why a reflex is fast.** The impulse does **not** go to the conscious part of the brain to be thought about. It passes straight across through a **relay neurone** in the spinal cord, so the path is **short** and there are **few synapses** to cross. Some reflexes, such as the pupil and blink reflexes, pass through an unconscious part of the brain rather than the spinal cord, but the principle is the same: no conscious decision is involved.

That is the whole reason for the design, and it is the answer to *why is a reflex faster than a considered action*.

**What reflexes are for.** They **protect the body** from harm. The examples are worth having ready:

- **Pulling away** from something hot or sharp, before damage is done.
- The **pupil reflex**: in bright light the pupil constricts, protecting the retina.
- **Blinking** when something approaches the eye.
- The **knee-jerk** reflex, which helps maintain posture.

**Are you aware of it?** Yes — but **afterwards**. The impulse is also sent up to the brain, so you feel the pain a moment after your hand has already moved. That order is the point: the response happens **first**, and the awareness follows.

So a reflex is not unconscious in the sense of unnoticed. It is unconscious in the sense that **no decision was involved**.

steps.title: The brain, and how it is studied
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* This section covers spec points 2.10B to 2.12B; 2.11B and 2.12B are also **Higher tier**.

**Three structures** are named, and each has a distinct job:

- The **cerebral hemispheres** — the large folded part on top. They control **conscious thought, memory, language and intelligence**.
- The **cerebellum** — beneath and behind them. It controls **balance** and the **coordination of muscles and movement**.
- The **medulla oblongata** — where the brain meets the spinal cord. It controls **unconscious activities** such as **heart rate and breathing rate**.

A way to keep them apart: **cerebral for thinking**, **cerebellum for moving smoothly**, **medulla for the things you never think about at all**.

*(Higher tier, Biology only.)* **How the brain is studied.** The brain is **encased in the skull**, which makes it very difficult to access. Two kinds of scan overcome this, and the difference between them is examinable.

- A **CT scan** uses **X-rays** to build a detailed picture of the brain's **structure**. It shows **where** a tumour or a damaged region is.
- A **PET scan** uses a **radioactive tracer** to show which parts of the brain are **active**. It shows **function** — what a region is doing — and can do so while the person performs a task.

So **CT shows structure, PET shows function**. If a question asks how scientists work out **what a region does**, the answer is a **PET** scan; if it asks how they find **where** a tumour is, a **CT** scan.

Comparing scans of a patient with damage to a particular region against their symptoms is how much of what we know about brain function was worked out.

steps.title: Going deeper: why the nervous system is hard to treat
steps.body:
*(Higher tier, Biology only.)* Spec point 2.12B asks you to explain the **limitations** in treating damage and disease in the brain and nervous system. There are four reasons, and a good answer gives several rather than one.

**1. Access.** The brain is **encased in the skull**, and the spinal cord in the vertebral column. Reaching either means cutting through bone, and there is little room to work.

**2. Delicacy and complexity.** Brain tissue is extremely delicate, and regions are tightly packed. Surgery to remove a **tumour** risks damaging the healthy tissue around it, and what that tissue does may be irreplaceable. A tumour deep in the brain may be impossible to reach without going through something vital.

**3. The blood–brain barrier.** The brain's blood vessels are much less permeable than others, which protects it from toxins — but also means **many drugs cannot get through**. A drug that works elsewhere in the body may be useless against a brain tumour for that reason alone.

**4. Nerve cells do not readily repair.** Neurones in the CNS do **not regenerate** as other cells do. This is why **spinal injuries** are so serious: once the neurones carrying impulses past the injury are damaged, the connection between brain and body below that point is **permanently** lost, and paralysis is not reversible with current treatment.

That fourth point connects back to the rest of this unit. Mitosis repairs the body by making identical replacement cells — but the cells of the CNS do not divide to replace themselves in the way skin or gut lining does. It is also why **stem cells** are so interesting as a possible treatment for paralysis: they offer a route to new nerve cells where the body has none.

**On scans, one distinction does most of the work.** **CT shows structure; PET shows function.** If a question mentions **activity**, **while performing a task**, or **which region is used for**, the answer is PET. If it mentions **locating**, **a tumour**, or **damage**, the answer is CT.

**And a precision point on reflexes.** The impulse does not *avoid* the brain entirely — it is sent there too, which is why you feel the pain. What it avoids is **waiting for a conscious decision**. Saying *the brain is not involved* is not quite right; saying *the conscious brain is not involved in producing the response* is.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The **CNS** is the **brain and spinal cord**; the peripheral nervous system is the neurones running to and from it.
- A neurone has a **cell body**, **dendrites and dendron** (impulses **in**), an **axon** (impulses **out**), and a **myelin sheath**.
- The **myelin sheath insulates** the axon and **speeds up** transmission.
- **Sensory** neurones carry impulses to the CNS; **relay** neurones within it; **motor** neurones out to effectors.
- At a **synapse** the impulse cannot jump the gap: a **neurotransmitter** is released, **diffuses across**, and **binds to receptors**, triggering a new impulse.
- Synapses **slow** transmission slightly and make it **one way only**.
- The **reflex arc**: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → **relay neurone** → motor neurone → effector → response.
- A reflex is **fast** because the impulse does not go to the **conscious brain**: the path is short with few synapses.
- Reflexes **protect the body**; you become aware **afterwards**.
- **Biology only — the brain**: **cerebral hemispheres** for conscious thought, memory, language and intelligence; **cerebellum** for balance and coordination; **medulla oblongata** for unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing.
- **CT scans use X-rays and show structure; PET scans use a tracer and show function.**
- Treating the nervous system is limited by **access**, **delicacy**, the **blood–brain barrier**, and the fact that **neurones do not repair** — which is why spinal injuries are permanent.

questions.prompt: A person touches a hot object and pulls their hand away. Describe the reflex arc involved, naming each stage in order, and explain why the response is so fast.
questions.solution: The stimulus is the heat of the object. This is detected by a temperature receptor in the skin of the hand. The receptor generates an electrical impulse which travels along a sensory neurone to the central nervous system, in this case the spinal cord. Within the spinal cord the impulse passes to a relay neurone, which carries it across to a motor neurone. The motor neurone carries the impulse out to the effector, which is a muscle in the arm. The muscle contracts, and the response is that the hand is pulled away from the object. Between each pair of neurones there is a synapse, which the impulse crosses by the release of a neurotransmitter that diffuses across the gap and binds to receptors on the next neurone. The response is very fast because the impulse does not travel to the conscious part of the brain to be thought about. It passes straight across through the relay neurone in the spinal cord, so the pathway is short and there are only a few synapses to cross, each of which would slow the impulse slightly. The impulse is also sent to the brain, which is why the person feels the pain, but only after the hand has already moved.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The arc, in order.**

1. **Stimulus** — the heat of the object.
2. **Receptor** — a temperature receptor in the skin detects it.
3. **Sensory neurone** — carries the impulse to the **CNS**, here the spinal cord.
4. **Relay neurone** — passes it straight across, within the spinal cord.
5. **Motor neurone** — carries it out to the effector.
6. **Effector** — a muscle in the arm contracts.
7. **Response** — the hand is pulled away.

Between each pair of neurones is a **synapse**, crossed by a **neurotransmitter** that diffuses across and binds to **receptors**.

**Why it is fast.** The impulse does **not** travel to the **conscious** part of the brain to be considered. It passes straight across through the relay neurone, so the pathway is **short** with **few synapses** — and each synapse would slow it slightly.

One precision: the impulse **is** sent to the brain as well, which is why the person feels the pain — but only **after** the hand has moved. A reflex is not unnoticed; it is simply not decided.

questions.prompt: Explain why damage and disease in the brain and nervous system are difficult to treat, and describe how CT and PET scans help scientists investigate the brain.
questions.solution: There are several reasons why the brain and nervous system are difficult to treat. First, the brain is encased within the skull and the spinal cord within the vertebral column, so simply gaining access requires cutting through bone and there is very little room in which to work. Second, brain tissue is extremely delicate and the different regions are very tightly packed together, so an operation to remove a tumour risks damaging healthy tissue nearby, and the functions of that tissue may not be replaceable. Third, the blood vessels of the brain are much less permeable than those elsewhere, forming what is called the blood brain barrier, so many drugs simply cannot reach the brain at all. Fourth, neurones in the central nervous system do not regenerate in the way that many other cells do, which is why a spinal injury usually causes permanent paralysis: once the neurones carrying impulses past the injury are destroyed, the connection between the brain and the body below it cannot be restored. Scans help because they allow the brain to be investigated without opening the skull. A CT scan uses X-rays to produce a detailed image of the structure of the brain, and can therefore show where a tumour or an area of damage is located. A PET scan uses a radioactive tracer to show which parts of the brain are active, and so shows function rather than structure, and it can be carried out while the person performs a task.

**Why treatment is difficult** — give several reasons, not one:

1. **Access.** The brain is **encased in the skull**, the cord in the vertebral column. Reaching either means cutting through bone, with little room to work.
2. **Delicacy and complexity.** Tissue is fragile and regions are tightly packed, so removing a **tumour** risks damaging healthy tissue whose function may be irreplaceable.
3. **The blood–brain barrier.** The brain's blood vessels are far **less permeable**, so **many drugs cannot reach it** at all.
4. **No repair.** Neurones in the CNS **do not regenerate**. Once those carrying impulses past a spinal injury are destroyed, the connection between brain and body below it is **permanently** lost — which is why paralysis from spinal injury is not currently reversible.

**How scans help.** Both allow the brain to be studied **without opening the skull**.

- A **CT scan** uses **X-rays** to image the brain's **structure**, showing **where** a tumour or damaged area is.
- A **PET scan** uses a **radioactive tracer** to show which regions are **active**, so it shows **function** — and can be done while the person performs a task.

**CT for structure, PET for function** is the distinction to carry into the exam.

questions.prompt: Which part of a neurone carries the impulse away from the cell body?
questions.solution: The **axon** carries the impulse **away** from the cell body. The **dendron** and dendrites carry it **towards** the cell body; the nucleus sits in the cell body, and a synapse is the gap between two neurones.

markScheme.description: the axon

questions.prompt: Which kind of neurone has a long dendron, a short axon and its cell body part-way along?
questions.solution: A **sensory neurone**: its long dendron brings the impulse from the receptor, and a short axon takes it into the CNS. A motor neurone has a **long axon** and its cell body inside the CNS; a relay neurone is short and lies wholly inside the CNS.

markScheme.description: a sensory neurone

questions.prompt: What is a sensory receptor?
questions.solution: A **sensory receptor** is a cell, or group of cells, that **detects a stimulus** and converts it into an **electrical impulse**. A muscle or gland that responds is an **effector**; the chemical is a **neurotransmitter**; the neurone inside the CNS is a **relay** neurone.

markScheme.description: detects a stimulus and converts it into an impulse

options: A muscle or gland that responds to an impulse
A chemical that carries a signal across a synapse gap
A neurone that passes impulses on inside the CNS
A cell that detects a stimulus and makes an impulse

questions.prompt: The blink reflex is coordinated in the brain, not in the spinal cord. Why is it still a reflex?
questions.solution: A reflex is defined by being **automatic**, with **no conscious decision**, not by where it is coordinated. The blink and pupil reflexes pass through an **unconscious part of the brain**, just as withdrawing a hand passes through the spinal cord.

markScheme.description: automatic, with no conscious decision

options: It uses a single neurone, with no synapses
It is automatic, with no conscious decision
The impulse never reaches any part of the brain
It is learned by practice in early childhood

questions.prompt: Which type of neurone carries an impulse from the central nervous system out to an effector such as a muscle?
questions.solution: **A motor neurone.** Its cell body lies inside the central nervous system and its long axon runs out to the effector, a muscle or a gland. A sensory neurone carries impulses the other way, from a receptor into the CNS; a relay neurone lies wholly inside the CNS and connects the two; and a sensory receptor is not a neurone at all but the cell that detects the stimulus in the first place.

markScheme.description: motor neurone

questions.prompt: A stroke damages part of a patient's cerebrum (the cerebral hemispheres) but leaves the cerebellum and the medulla oblongata intact. Which statement is consistent with this?
questions.solution: **Each region has its own job.** The cerebrum, made of the two cerebral hemispheres, is responsible for conscious thought, memory, language and voluntary movement, so damage there can affect speech, memory or the control of movement. The cerebellum controls balance and the coordination of muscle movement, and the medulla oblongata controls heart rate and breathing; both are intact, so those functions carry on. Regions cannot simply take over each other's work, which is why damage to one shows as a loss of its particular functions.

markScheme.description: heart rate and breathing (medulla) continue; memory, speech or conscious movement (cerebrum) may be affected

options: Breathing stops unless a machine takes over, because breathing is controlled by the cerebral hemispheres
Only balance and coordination are lost, because those are controlled by the cerebral hemispheres
Heart rate and breathing carry on normally, but memory, speech or conscious movement may be affected
Nothing changes, because every region of the brain can take over any function of any other region

questions.prompt: A drug blocks the receptors on the second neurone at a synapse. Which statement describes the effect of the drug on transmission across that synapse?
questions.skill: neurotransmitters and receptors at a synapse
questions.solution: **The signal stops at the synapse.** When an impulse arrives at the end of the first neurone, a neurotransmitter is released and diffuses across the gap; a new impulse starts in the next neurone only when the neurotransmitter binds to receptors on it. With the receptors blocked, everything up to the binding still happens, but the final step does not, so no impulse is triggered. An electrical impulse cannot jump the gap, which is why a chemical is used at all; the first neurone has no way of sensing the receptors opposite; and a signal cannot travel backwards, because only the first side releases neurotransmitter and only the second side has receptors.

markScheme.description: neurotransmitter is released and diffuses across but cannot bind, so no impulse starts in the next neurone

options: The electrical impulse jumps straight across the gap instead, so transmission becomes much faster than it was before the drug
Neurotransmitter is still released and diffuses across the gap, but it cannot bind, so no impulse starts in the next neurone
The first neurone stops releasing any neurotransmitter, because it can detect that the receptors opposite it are blocked
Impulses begin to travel backwards across the synapse, because the usual forward route through the receptors is blocked

questions.prompt: A scan shows a tumour deep inside a patient's brain, pressing against the medulla oblongata. The surgeons decide not to operate. Which statement best explains their decision?
questions.solution: **The risk to the tissue around it.** The medulla oblongata controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing rate, and brain tissue is delicate and tightly packed, so surgery to remove the tumour could damage it. Neurones in the central nervous system do not regenerate, so any damage done would be permanent and could be fatal. The tumour itself is a mass of cells dividing without control, so it will grow if left; the blood-brain barrier is a feature of the brain's blood vessels that stops many drugs reaching the brain, not a barrier to instruments; and no part of the brain removes tumours by itself.

markScheme.description: removing it risks damaging the tissue controlling heart rate and breathing, which does not regenerate

options: Tumours in the brain do not grow, because brain cells cannot divide, so a tumour this deep can safely be left where it is
The blood-brain barrier would stop the surgeons reaching the tumour, because surgical instruments cannot cross it
Removing it risks damaging the surrounding tissue, which controls heart rate and breathing and does not regenerate
The medulla oblongata is the one part of the brain that repairs itself, so the tumour will be broken down naturally

questions.prompt: Name the chemical that is released into the gap at a synapse when an electrical impulse arrives at the end of a neurone.
questions.solution: **A neurotransmitter.** The electrical impulse cannot jump the gap, so the first neurone releases this chemical, which diffuses across the synapse and binds to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse there.

markScheme.description: neurotransmitter

questions.prompt: An electrical impulse travels along a motor neurone 0.9 m long, from the spinal cord to a muscle in the foot, in 0.015 s. Calculate the speed of the impulse in metres per second.
questions.solution: Speed $= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{0.9}{0.015} = 60$ m/s. A single motor neurone can run the whole way from the spinal cord to the foot, and its myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds the impulse along it.

markScheme.description: divides the distance by the time
60 m/s

questions.prompt: In a reflex arc, an impulse travels 0.75 m along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord at 50 m/s, crosses two synapses that each take 0.5 ms (the relay neurone between them is so short that the time along it can be ignored), and then travels 0.75 m along a motor neurone to a muscle at 100 m/s. Calculate the total time taken from receptor to muscle, in milliseconds.
questions.solution: Time along each neurone is distance ÷ speed. Sensory neurone: $\dfrac{0.75}{50} = 0.015$ s $= 15$ ms. Motor neurone: $\dfrac{0.75}{100} = 0.0075$ s $= 7.5$ ms. The two synapses add $2 \times 0.5 = 1$ ms. Total $= 15 + 7.5 + 1 = 23.5$ ms. The synapses are a small part of the total here, which is why a reflex with only two of them is fast: a path through the conscious brain would be longer and would cross many more.

markScheme.description: converts each neurone's distance and speed to a time: 15 ms and 7.5 ms
adds the two synapse delays, 1 ms

questions.prompt: Describe how a sensory receptor and a sensory neurone together carry information about a stimulus to the central nervous system.
questions.solution: A sensory receptor is a cell, or group of cells, that **detects a stimulus**, such as heat on the skin, and **converts it into an electrical impulse**. The impulse passes along the sensory neurone's **long dendron** towards the cell body, which lies part-way along the neurone, and on along its short **axon** into the central nervous system, the brain or spinal cord. The **myelin sheath** around the fibre insulates it, so the impulse does not leak to neighbouring neurones, and speeds up transmission.

markScheme.description: the receptor detects the stimulus and converts it into an electrical impulse
the impulse travels along the sensory neurone's long dendron, past the cell body and along the axon into the CNS
the myelin sheath insulates the fibre and speeds up transmission

criteria.text: Says that the sensory receptor detects the stimulus and converts it into an electrical impulse
Says that the impulse travels along the sensory neurone's long dendron, past the cell body part-way along, and along its axon into the brain or spinal cord
Says that the myelin sheath insulates the fibre and speeds up transmission

questions.modelAnswer: A sensory receptor is a cell, or a group of cells, that detects a particular stimulus: temperature receptors in the skin detect heat, and light-sensitive cells in the retina detect light. When the stimulus arrives, the receptor converts it into an electrical impulse. The impulse enters the sensory neurone and travels along its long dendron towards the cell body, which in a sensory neurone sits part-way along the fibre rather than at one end. From the cell body it continues along the short axon into the central nervous system, the spinal cord or the brain, where it is passed to a relay neurone. The fibre is wrapped in a myelin sheath, a fatty layer that insulates the axon so the impulse does not leak into neighbouring neurones and that makes the impulse travel much faster than it would along a bare fibre. The length of the neurone matters too: one sensory neurone can carry the impulse all the way from a fingertip to the spinal cord without passing it on.

questions.prompt: A patient has frequent seizures. A CT scan of her brain appears normal. Explain why a PET scan might still reveal which region of the brain is responsible, and why doctors might nonetheless decide not to remove that region.
questions.skill: CT against PET, and the limits of surgery
questions.solution: A CT scan uses X-rays to show the **structure** of the brain, so it reveals a region that is the wrong shape or size, such as a tumour. A region that looks normal but is working abnormally shows nothing on it. A PET scan uses a **radioactive tracer** to show which regions are **active**, so it shows function, and a region that is unusually active during a seizure can be located. Even so, removing it may not be possible: brain tissue is delicate and tightly packed, so surgery risks damaging the healthy tissue around it, and the functions of that tissue may be irreplaceable because neurones in the central nervous system do not regenerate.

markScheme.description: CT shows structure, so a region of normal structure but abnormal function does not show on it
PET uses a tracer to show how active each region is, so the region with abnormal activity can be located
removal risks damaging the delicate tissue around it, whose function cannot be replaced because neurones do not regenerate

criteria.text: Explains that a CT scan uses X-rays to show structure, so a region that is normal in structure but abnormal in function shows nothing

Explains that a PET scan uses a radioactive tracer to show how active each region is, so a region whose activity is abnormal, higher or lower than normal, can be located even though its structure looks normal
Explains that removing it risks damaging the delicate, tightly packed tissue around it, whose functions may be irreplaceable because neurones in the CNS do not regenerate

questions.modelAnswer: The two scans answer different questions. A CT scan uses X-rays to build a picture of the brain's structure: it shows where things are and what shape they have, which is why it finds a tumour or a damaged region. The region causing this patient's seizures may be perfectly normal in shape and size, so a CT scan shows nothing wrong. A PET scan works differently. A radioactive tracer is injected and the scan shows where in the brain it is being used, which reveals which regions are active. The responsible region shows up with abnormal activity, higher or lower than the regions around it, even though it looks structurally normal, so the PET scan can locate it where the CT scan could not. Finding it does not mean it can be removed. Brain tissue is extremely delicate and the regions are tightly packed, so an operation risks damaging the healthy tissue around the target, and that tissue may control something essential, such as speech or movement. Neurones in the central nervous system do not regenerate, so any damage done during surgery would be permanent. The doctors have to weigh the harm of the seizures against the risk of a permanent loss, and may decide the operation is not worth it.

questions.prompt: A student wants to find out whether listening to loud music changes a person's reaction time. In the ruler-drop test, a partner holds a ruler vertically with the zero mark level with the top of the person's open thumb and forefinger, drops it without warning, and the person catches it as quickly as possible; the distance fallen is read off and converted to a reaction time using a conversion table. Devise a plan for the investigation, identifying the independent, dependent and control variables, and explain how the results should be processed before a conclusion is drawn.
questions.skill: investigating reaction times: planning and processing
questions.solution: The **independent variable** is whether loud music is playing, through headphones, or not; the **dependent variable** is the distance the ruler falls, converted to a reaction time. Everything else is **controlled**: the same person, the same hand, the ruler held with the zero mark at the top of the thumb each time, no warning before the drop, and the same time of day. People get quicker with **practice**, so a few practice drops come first and the two conditions are alternated rather than done one after the other. Each condition is **repeated** at least five to ten times, anomalous results are discarded, and a **mean** is found. Each distance is converted to a time with the table, because a shorter fall means a shorter reaction time. The two means are compared, and a difference counts only if it is larger than the **spread** within each set of repeats. The time being measured is the time for the impulse to pass from the receptors in the eye, along sensory neurones to the brain, and out along motor neurones to the hand muscles: a conscious response, not a reflex.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): describes doing the ruler-drop test with and without music, naming a variable or two, with little on control or on processing the results

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): identifies the independent and dependent variables, gives relevant control variables, and either repeats with a mean or converts distance to time, but the plan or the processing is incomplete

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a complete plan with the variables identified and controlled, practice drops and alternating conditions to allow for learning, several repeats with anomalies discarded and means compared, distances converted to times, and a conclusion that weighs the difference between the means against the spread of the repeats

criteria.text: Identifies the independent variable, whether loud music is playing (through headphones) or not, and the dependent variable, the distance the ruler falls, converted to a reaction time

Gives control variables: the same person, the same hand and starting position with the zero mark at the top of the thumb, the same ruler, no warning before the drop, and the same conditions otherwise, such as time of day
Allows for practice: a few practice drops first, and the two conditions alternated or in a random order, so that improvement with practice does not favour whichever condition is tested second
Repeats each condition at least five to ten times, discards any anomalous result, and calculates a mean distance or mean time for each condition
Converts each distance to a reaction time with the conversion table, since a shorter fall means a shorter reaction time, so that the two conditions are compared as times
Draws the conclusion carefully: a difference between the means counts only if it is larger than the spread within each set of repeats

questions.modelAnswer:
**The variables.** The independent variable is whether or not loud music is playing, which is best delivered through headphones so that the volume is the same on every trial. The dependent variable is the distance the ruler falls before it is caught, which is converted to a reaction time using the conversion table. Everything else is kept the same: the same person is tested throughout, using the same hand; the partner holds the same ruler vertically with the zero mark level with the top of the open thumb and forefinger every time; the ruler is dropped without warning; and both conditions are tested at the same time of day, in the same room, so that tiredness and distraction do not differ between them.

**Allowing for practice.** People get quicker at catching the ruler as they get used to it. If all the trials without music were done first and all the trials with music second, any improvement would wrongly look like an effect of the music. So the person has a few practice drops before any result is recorded, and the two conditions are then alternated, or taken in a random order, so that practice affects both equally.

**Repeats.** Each condition is tested at least five to ten times. A single catch can be lucky or distracted, so repeats are essential. Any result far from the others, such as a drop where the person was not ready, is treated as anomalous and left out, and a mean is calculated for each condition.

**Processing.** Each distance is converted to a reaction time with the table, because distance is only a stand-in for what is actually being measured, and a shorter fall means a shorter reaction time. Every distance is converted to a time and the mean time is found for each condition; converting the mean distance instead gives a slightly different answer, because the conversion is not a simple proportion. The two mean reaction times are then compared.

**The conclusion.** A difference between the two means shows an effect of the music only if it is larger than the spread of the repeats within each condition. If the repeats without music range from 0.17 s to 0.23 s, a difference between the means of 0.01 s is not evidence of anything, while a difference of 0.05 s would be. The time being measured is the time for an impulse to pass from the light receptors in the eye, along sensory neurones to the brain, where the decision to catch is made, and out along motor neurones to the muscles of the hand. Because the brain's conscious decision is involved, this is a reaction and not a reflex, and that is why it can be affected by attention, practice and distraction in a way a reflex such as the knee jerk cannot.

examTechnique.body:
Give the reflex arc in order and name every stage, including the stimulus and the response.

Name the effector specifically: a muscle in the arm, not just an effector.

For a synapse, use the words neurotransmitter, diffuses and receptors. All three carry marks.

When explaining why a reflex is fast, say the impulse does not go to the conscious brain, and mention the short path and few synapses.

For the brain, match the structure to its function precisely: cerebral hemispheres think, cerebellum coordinates, medulla runs the unconscious body.

For scans, decide whether the question is about structure or function before choosing CT or PET.
examinerErrors: Saying the impulse jumps across the synapse.
Leaving out the relay neurone from a reflex arc.
Naming a neurone as the effector rather than a muscle or gland.
Saying the brain is not involved in a reflex at all.
Confusing the cerebellum with the cerebral hemispheres.
Saying a CT scan shows which regions are active.
Saying the myelin sheath carries the impulse.
Giving only one reason why the nervous system is hard to treat.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer gives the reflex arc as a complete path with the effector named specifically, and explains the speed in terms of the pathway rather than asserting that reflexes are fast. It describes the synapse as a change from electrical to chemical and back, which makes both the delay and the one-way property obvious rather than memorised. On the brain it matches each structure to its function without hesitation and chooses the right scan by asking whether the question is about structure or function. Asked why treatment is limited, it gives several reasons and connects the failure of neurones to regenerate back to mitosis and to stem cells.
